{"id": "7716e8de-409e-4a62-bb60-afd1627640d7", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_1hWoVbuKYZjuiTT2ppXMk3", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3\",\"context\":\"## Types of VPC endpoints for Amazon S3\\n\\nYou can use two types of VPC endpoints to access Amazon S3: *gateway\\nendpoints* and *interface endpoints* (by using AWS PrivateLink).\\nA *gateway endpoint* is a gateway that you specify in your\\nroute table to access Amazon S3 from your VPC over the AWS network. *Interface endpoints* extend the functionality of gateway endpoints by using\\nprivate IP addresses to route requests to Amazon S3 from within your VPC, on premises, or from a\\nVPC in another AWS Region by using VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway. For\\nmore information, see What is VPC peering? and Transit Gateway vs VPC peering.\\n\\nInterface endpoints are compatible with gateway endpoints. If you have an existing gateway\\nendpoint in the VPC, you can use both types of endpoints in the same VPC.\\n\\n| Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 | Interface endpoints for Amazon S3 |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| In both cases, your network traffic remains on the AWS network. | |\\n| Use Amazon S3 public IP addresses | Use private IP addresses from your VPC to access Amazon S3 |\\n| Use the same Amazon S3 DNS names | Require endpoint-specific Amazon S3 DNS names |\\n| Do not allow access from on premises | Allow access from on premises |\\n| Do not allow access from another AWS Region | Allow access from a VPC in another AWS Region by using VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway |\\n| Not billed | Billed |\\n\\nFor more information, see Gateway endpoints and interface VPC endpoints in the\\n*AWS PrivateLink Guide*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/privatelink-interface-endpoints.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Amazon S3 FAQs\",\"context\":\"#### What is an Amazon VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3?\\n\\nAn Amazon VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 is a logical entity within a VPC that allows connectivity to S3 over the AWS global network. There are two types of VPC endpoints for S3: gateway VPC endpoints and interface VPC endpoints. Gateway endpoints are a gateway that you specify in your route table to access S3 from your VPC over the AWS network. Interface endpoints extend the functionality of gateway endpoints by using private IPs to route requests to S3 from within your VPC, on-premises, or from a different AWS Region. For more information, visit the AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3 documentation\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/s3/faqs/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Choosing Your VPC Endpoint Strategy for Amazon S3 | AWS Architecture Blog\",\"context\":\"## VPC endpoint overview\\n\\nA VPC endpoint is a virtual scalable networking component you create in a VPC and use as a private entry point to supported AWS services and third-party applications. Currently, two types of VPC endpoints can be used to connect to Amazon S3: interface VPC endpoint and gateway VPC endpoint.\\n\\nWhen you configure an interface VPC endpoint, an elastic network interface (ENI) with a private IP address is deployed in your subnet. An Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC can communicate with an Amazon S3 bucket through the ENI and AWS network. Using the interface endpoint, applications in your on-premises data center can easily query S3 buckets over AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN. Interface endpoint supports a growing list of AWS services. Consult our documentation to find AWS services compatible with interface endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink.\\n\\nGateway VPC endpoints use prefix lists as the IP route target in a VPC route table. This routes traffic privately to Amazon S3 or Amazon DynamoDB. An EC2 instance in a VPC without internet access can still directly read from and/or write to an Amazon S3 bucket. Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3 are the services currently accessible via gateway endpoints.\\n\\nYour internal security policies may have strict rules against communication between your VPC and the internet. To maintain compliance with these policies, you can use VPC endpoint to connect to AWS public services like Amazon S3. To control user or application access to the VPC endpoint and the resources it supports, you can use an AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) resource policy. This will separately secure the VPC endpoint and accessible resources\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/choosing-your-vpc-endpoint-strategy-for-amazon-s3/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up AWS docs on S3 gateway vs interface VPC endpoints"}

{"id": "7f8fef16-170e-4985-8474-28c41bf47ae7", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both let you reach S3 without traversing the public internet, but they work quite differently:

**Gateway endpoint**
- Implemented as a route table entry (target) in your VPC — not a network interface
- Traffic uses S3's public IP addresses, but stays on the AWS network
- Uses the same S3 DNS names you'd normally use
- Only reachable from within the VPC itself — no access from on-premises networks, and no access from a VPC in another region (even via peering/Transit Gateway)
- Free — no hourly or data processing charges

**Interface endpoint (via AWS PrivateLink)**
- Deployed as an elastic network interface (ENI) with a private IP in your subnet
- Traffic routes to S3 using that private IP
- Requires endpoint-specific DNS names
- Can be reached from on-premises (via Direct Connect or VPN) and from a VPC in another region (via peering or Transit Gateway)
- Billed — hourly charge plus data processing charges

Both are compatible and can coexist in the same VPC. The common pattern: use the free gateway endpoint for in-VPC traffic, and add an interface endpoint only when you need on-prem or cross-region private access to S3.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
